cross.h: Plans look more alike than different
cross.t: In every region, people-first strategies make up 34 to 49% of the latest national plan, and growth strategies 30 to 43%. Only one framework family sits more than about 4 points above or below the all-country average: natural capital in Egypt's plan. Regions differ in what they lean toward, not in the shape of the tree.

cross.h: Climate is the storm almost every region names
cross.t: Climate change is the risk tied to the most strategies in seven of the eight regions, for example 17% of strategies in South-East Asia and 16% in South Asia and the Pacific. In the Arab States, environmental degradation edges it out. Yet the climate framework family itself holds only about 5% of strategies, so the risk is named more often than it is answered.

cross.h: Governments plan and coordinate, but rarely look ahead
cross.t: Strategies on development planning and on coordination across government appear in many plans. Strategic foresight and scenario work appear in only a handful, and the Anticipation and Strategic Foresight subpillar holds about 3% of strategies. These three levers were restored on 25 November, and strategies were placed on them by their wording rather than by a fresh mapping run.

cross.h: Plans act through organisations, rarely through money
cross.t: Almost half of all strategies (46%) work through organisations: programmes, agencies and capacity. Another 28% work through information and 18% through rules. Only 8% use money, such as grants, subsidies or tax measures, and only 4% do in the Pacific. Spending choices show up in budgets, not in the plans.

Only a quarter of strategies (25%) carry a quantified target, and fewer than one in five (19%) say how they will be monitored. South Asia (34%) and East Asia (32%) come highest on targets, and Latin America and the Caribbean and the Arab States come lowest (14% each). This holds back the RHDR Making Change Happen pillar everywhere.

South-East Asia.h: Growth through clusters, skills and jobs, lighter on health
b: The region's plans favour linkages, clusters and cities (6.2% against 5.1%), knowledge (7.2% against 6.6%) and rapid resource mobilisation (3.9% against 3.1%). Jobs, places and mobility is above the average in 7 of 9 countries.
Health is light: long and healthy life is 4.2% against 5.1%, and only one country is above the average. Climate change is the risk named most, tied to 17% of strategies.
Across seven countries' plan series, later plans put more on delivery capability (up about 1 point) and less on capabilities and domestic integration.

South Asia.h: The most specific plans, leaning to skills, trade and accountable government
b: South Asian plans are the easiest to place: 67% of strategies reach a lever (63% on average), and 34% carry a quantified target (25% on average).
They lean to authorised flexibility (above the average in 7 of 9 countries), knowledge, reaching foreign markets and accountability. They put less on enterprise finance and on upgrading.
Across seven plan series, delivery capability is rising (up about 2 points) and domestic integration is falling (down about 3 points).

East Asia.h: Upgrading for export, under ageing and technology pressure
b: Export-led strategies make up 13% of the latest plans (8% on average). Upgrading and innovation (9.3% against 5.1%) and linkages, clusters and cities are above the average in 4 of 5 countries. In plan series, export-led growth is rising (up about 5 points).

This is the only region where demographic shifts are among the top risks (12% of strategies), alongside technological change (13%) and climate (14%). It also has the most strategies marked high urgency (35% against 19%).
Enterprise finance is below the average in every country, and authorised flexibility is light. The five countries are China, Japan, Mongolia, South Korea and Taiwan.

Pacific.h: Plans for protection and stewardship, less for export growth
b: Future generations, the subpillar holding climate, natural capital and resilience, is 15% of strategies against 13%. Climate is above the average in 7 of 10 countries.
Market rules and property rights stand out in all 10 countries, and economic and human wealth in 7. Land and resource tenure runs through Pacific plans.
Export-led growth is half the average (4% against 8%), upgrading and innovation is light (2.6% against 5.1%), and only 4% of strategies use money as the instrument.

Europe and Central Asia.h: Competitiveness, connectivity and money on the table
b: Growth strategies make up 43% of the latest plans, the highest of any region. Infrastructure and connectivity (7.6% against 4.4%, all three countries above the average), rural producers, reaching foreign markets and enterprise finance lead.
These plans use money more than any other region (19% of strategies against 8%), and 70% of their strategies reach a lever.
Three countries are read here: Kazakhstan, Poland and Serbia. Estonia's and Uzbekistan's documents yield too few strategies to count.

Arab States.h: Resource stewardship and broad economic goals
b: Natural capital is twice the average (12.4% against 6.0%). Environmental degradation, resource pressures and climate are the leading risks (14 to 15% of strategies each).
Enterprise finance (6.2% against 3.5%) and broad economic goals that fit no family (12%) are large, while governance is light.

This reads as Egypt's Vision 2030 alone. The documents for Morocco, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates yield too few strategies to count, so treat this as a country note, not a regional message.

Africa.h: Living standards, trade and data, with fewer transformative strategies
b: Decent standard of living (8.3% against 6.9%) and rural producers lean above the average. Reaching foreign markets (3.5% against 2.4%) and data sharing (2.3% against 1.1%) are above the average in 4 of 5 countries.
Natural capital (4.5% against 6.0%), climate and infrastructure are light. Fewer strategies are framed as transformative than anywhere except the Arab States (17% against 22%).
Five countries are read here: Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria and Rwanda. Their national plans and some budgets are in, but no sector plans or UNGA statements.

Latin America and the Caribbean.h: The most people-first plans, aimed at exclusion and places
b: People-first strategies make up 49% of the latest plans, the highest of any region. Tackling structural exclusion is more than double the average (10% against 4%). Spaces, decent standard of living and markets are above the average in all five countries.
Infrastructure, authorised flexibility and enterprise finance are light.
The fewest strategies are tied to a risk (28% against 37%), and the fewest carry a quantified target (14%). The five countries are Brazil, Colombia, Jamaica, Peru and Uruguay.
